% Abstract — collapse_severity_monitor
% Data sources: plan006 (3-seed Cohen's d), within_gen_analysis, plan003-fullft-05B

\begin{abstract}
Iterative training on model-generated data causes model collapse---progressive loss of distribution tails, contraction of output diversity, and degradation of acquired knowledge---yet the metrics practitioners most commonly watch during training fail to detect it.
We systematically evaluate four families of training-time signals---spectral (stable rank, spectral entropy), output (train loss, evaluation perplexity, token entropy), gradient (L2 norm), and downstream (HellaSwag accuracy)---as collapse severity monitors across five experimental configurations spanning model scales (0.5B--3B), fine-tuning methods (QLoRA, full fine-tuning), contamination fractions ($\alpha \in \{0, 0.1, \ldots, 1.0\}$), and text domains (WikiText-2, PubMed).
We find that different signal families have complementary operating ranges.
Spectral entropy achieves the largest cross-generation effect size (Cohen's $d = 33.48$, $\mathrm{CV} = 0.0015$ across seeds), while stable rank provides the strongest within-generation early warning ($\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.94$ at 10\% training progress, $0.984$ pooled, 34.4\% deviation at 3\% of training).
Held-out evaluation perplexity provides no within-generation early warning (pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.533$, indistinguishable from random), while train loss is an effective but interpretively ambiguous detector (pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.923$): its decrease reflects successful fitting of corrupted data, not improved model quality.
The same signal can be informative under one training method and misleading under another: gradient norm is non-monotonic under QLoRA but monotonic under full fine-tuning.
These findings yield a three-tier monitoring strategy---stable rank for within-generation alarms, evaluation perplexity for cross-generation tracking, spectral entropy for severity discrimination---and a signal taxonomy characterizing where each family succeeds, saturates, or misleads.
\end{abstract}

Our study has several limitations that bound the scope of our conclusions.

\paragraph{Scale.}
Our primary experiments use Qwen2.5-0.5B and 1.5B models, with only a single-seed spot-check at 3B.
Whether signal--severity relationships and operating ranges transfer to models at scales of practical deployment ($\geq$7B) remains unvalidated.
Stable rank baselines are known to be scale-dependent~\citep{Jha2025}, and threshold calibration may require per-scale adjustment.

\paragraph{Seed count and statistical power.}
Cross-generation effect sizes are computed from $N = 3$ seeds (C2 configuration, interim 3 of 5 planned seeds); within-generation AUROC results use $N = 1$ seed at 0.5B (C1).
The full fine-tuning comparison (C4) uses $N = 1$ seed.
These sample sizes are insufficient for rank-based tests (minimum $p = 0.25$ for Wilcoxon with $N = 3$), and we rely on bootstrap confidence intervals.
Stable rank's coefficient of variation ($\mathrm{CV} = 0.022$) is an order of magnitude larger than spectral entropy's ($0.0015$), and its effect size dropped from $d = 61.7$ to $d = 9.43$ when a third seed was added---underscoring that our ranking of signals by sensitivity may shift with more seeds.

\paragraph{Domain coverage.}
We evaluate on WikiText-2 and PubMed abstracts.
Whether our signal taxonomy generalizes to code, dialogue, multilingual text, or instruction-following data is unknown.

\paragraph{Collapse source.}
Our iterative retraining protocol simulates a specific collapse mechanism---self-consuming loops with controlled contamination fractions.
Real-world collapse may involve mixed provenance (multiple model generations), distribution shift between generations, or partial synthetic contamination at unknown fractions.
Signal behavior under these conditions may differ from our controlled setting.

\paragraph{Fine-tuning methods.}
We compare QLoRA and full fine-tuning.
Other parameter-efficient methods (LoRA without quantization, adapters, prefix tuning) may interact differently with spectral signals due to different parameterization constraints.

\paragraph{Causal claims.}
We establish correlations between signals and collapse severity, not causal mechanisms.
The spectral entropy increase under collapse reflects a change in representation structure, but we do not prove that this change causes (rather than accompanies) output degradation.

4	\section{Introduction}
5	\label{sec:introduction}
6	
7	As LLM-generated text pervades web-scraped training corpora, practitioners increasingly fine-tune models on data shaped by prior model generations.
8	This recursive dynamic creates self-consuming loops that cause \emph{model collapse}---progressive loss of distribution tails, contraction of output diversity, and degradation of acquired knowledge~\citep{Shumailov2024,Alemohammad2024}.
9	The problem compounds: even trace synthetic contamination induces collapse at sufficient depth~\citep{Dohmatob2025}, with errors accumulating across iterations at accelerating rates~\citep{Dohmatob2024_tails,Fu2024_icml}.
10	Yet the metric practitioners most commonly rely on for quality assessment---held-out evaluation perplexity---fails to detect this degradation within a run, achieving pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.533$ for within-generation collapse detection (indistinguishable from random chance).
11	Train loss does change under collapse (pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.923$), but its decrease is interpretively ambiguous: the model fits lower-entropy synthetic data more easily, which looks like healthy convergence.
12	A practitioner watching only perplexity or interpreting train loss at face value would have no reliable warning that collapse is underway.
13	
14	Existing work addresses model collapse from two directions.
15	On the theoretical side, \citet{Shumailov2024} established the phenomenon, \citet{Dohmatob2025} proved that any nonzero synthetic fraction eventually induces strong collapse, and \citet{Dohmatob2024_tails} showed that collapse alters neural scaling laws.
16	On the mitigation side, data accumulation~\citep{Gerstgrasser2024}, loss modification~\citep{Zibakhsh2025}, and verification-based filtering~\citep{Feng2025} each reduce collapse pressure under specific conditions.
17	Missing from this landscape is a systematic analysis of which \emph{training-time signals} best track collapse severity, when they provide early warning, and where they saturate or actively mislead.
18	\citet{Schaeffer2025} highlight that even the definition of collapse varies across studies, further motivating signal-level analysis grounded in controlled experiments.
19	The two closest concurrent works---SIGMA~\citep{Gu2026}, which monitors output embedding spectra, and the topological index of \citet{Kalinowski2026}---each address part of this gap but carry limitations: SIGMA requires a clean reference distribution and operates post-hoc; topological monitoring incurs higher computational cost.
20	Neither provides a cross-family comparison of signal operating ranges or quantitative within-generation early warning thresholds.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

As LLM-generated text pervades web-scraped training corpora, practitioners increasingly fine-tune models on data shaped by prior model generations.
This recursive dynamic creates self-consuming loops that cause \emph{model collapse}---progressive loss of distribution tails, contraction of output diversity, and degradation of acquired knowledge~\citep{Shumailov2024,Alemohammad2024}.
The problem compounds: even trace synthetic contamination induces collapse at sufficient depth~\citep{Dohmatob2025}, with errors accumulating across iterations at accelerating rates~\citep{Dohmatob2024_tails,Fu2024_icml}.
Yet the metric practitioners most commonly rely on for quality assessment---held-out evaluation perplexity---fails to detect this degradation within a run, achieving pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.533$ for within-generation collapse detection (indistinguishable from random chance).
Train loss does change under collapse (pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.923$), but its decrease is interpretively ambiguous: the model fits lower-entropy synthetic data more easily, which looks like healthy convergence.
A practitioner watching only perplexity or interpreting train loss at face value would have no reliable warning that collapse is underway.

Existing work addresses model collapse from two directions.
On the theoretical side, \citet{Shumailov2024} established the phenomenon, \citet{Dohmatob2025} proved that any nonzero synthetic fraction eventually induces strong collapse, and \citet{Dohmatob2024_tails} showed that collapse alters neural scaling laws.
On the mitigation side, data accumulation~\citep{Gerstgrasser2024}, loss modification~\citep{Zibakhsh2025}, and verification-based filtering~\citep{Feng2025} each reduce collapse pressure under specific conditions.
Missing from this landscape is a systematic analysis of which \emph{training-time signals} best track collapse severity, when they provide early warning, and where they saturate or actively mislead.
\citet{Schaeffer2025} highlight that even the definition of collapse varies across studies, further motivating signal-level analysis grounded in controlled experiments.
The two closest concurrent works---SIGMA~\citep{Gu2026}, which monitors output embedding spectra, and the topological index of \citet{Kalinowski2026}---each address part of this gap but carry limitations: SIGMA requires a clean reference distribution and operates post-hoc; topological monitoring incurs higher computational cost.
Neither provides a cross-family comparison of signal operating ranges or quantitative within-generation early warning thresholds.

We conduct a systematic empirical study of training-time signals as collapse severity monitors.
We evaluate four signal families---spectral (stable rank, spectral entropy), output (train loss, evaluation perplexity, token entropy), gradient (L2 norm), and downstream (HellaSwag accuracy)---across five experimental configurations spanning model scales (0.5B to 3B), fine-tuning methods (QLoRA and full fine-tuning), contamination fractions ($\alpha \in \{0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0\}$), and text domains (WikiText-2, PubMed).
Our central finding is that different signal families have complementary operating ranges, and the same signal's utility can flip from informative to misleading depending on the training method.

Our contributions:

\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Signal--severity correlation.}
    Spectral and output signals track collapse across contamination levels.
    Spectral entropy achieves the largest effect size (Cohen's $d = 33.48$, coefficient of variation $\mathrm{CV} = 0.0015$ across seeds), followed by evaluation perplexity ($d = 20.82$) and stable rank ($d = 9.43$, $\mathrm{CV} = 0.022$).

    The exception---gradient norm, which is non-monotonic under QLoRA but monotonic under full fine-tuning---demonstrates that method-dependence is a first-order concern for monitoring pipeline design.

    \item \textbf{Within-generation early warning and negative results.}
    Stable rank achieves $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.94$ at 10\% training progress ($0.984$ pooled) for binary collapse detection, with 34.4\% deviation from baseline at 3\% of training.
    Train loss provides the second-strongest within-generation signal (pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.923$), though its decrease reflects successful fitting of corrupted data rather than improved model quality.
    Held-out evaluation perplexity achieves pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.533$ for within-generation detection---the most commonly relied-upon quality metric fails at the most actionable task---and token entropy achieves pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.478$, providing no reliable discrimination despite a large initial deviation.
    Evaluation perplexity's failure has a structural explanation: it accumulates degradation through the iterative contamination loop, not within a single generation's training.

    \item \textbf{Signal taxonomy with method-dependent operating ranges.}
    Signal informativeness depends on the fine-tuning method and model scale.
    Gradient norm is non-monotonic under QLoRA but monotonic under full fine-tuning.
    HellaSwag accuracy is insensitive at 0.5B scale (relative change ${<}3\%$, $N{=}1$).
    Distinct-1 is non-monotonic, reversing direction between moderate and full contamination.
    Full fine-tuning produces sharper collapse onset ($15.3\times$ evaluation perplexity ratio at generation~1) than QLoRA ($8.7\times$) but lower terminal severity.
    These findings motivate a three-tier recommendation: stable rank for within-generation alarms, evaluation perplexity for cross-generation tracking, and spectral entropy for severity discrimination.
\end{enumerate}

Section~\ref{sec:related_work} surveys collapse theory, spectral analysis of neural networks, and concurrent monitoring approaches.
Section~\ref{sec:method} details our iterative contamination protocol, signal definitions, and evaluation framework.
Section~\ref{sec:results} presents signal--severity correlations, within-generation early warning analysis, and the method-dependent signal taxonomy.
Section~\ref{sec:discussion} discusses practical monitoring recommendations and limitations.
Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes.

34	Spearman correlations provide directional confirmation: spectral entropy maintains high $|\rho|$ across generations.

40	\label{sec:early_warning_results}
41	
42	Cross-generation tracking (Section~\ref{sec:correlation}) requires completing multiple generations to assess severity.
43	A more actionable capability is detecting collapse \emph{within} a single training run, enabling early stopping before degradation accumulates.
44	We evaluate this using the relative deviation $\Delta_s$ (Eq.~\ref{eq:deviation}) and AUROC for binary collapse detection at each checkpoint.
45	
46	\paragraph{Stable rank as early alarm.}
47	Stable rank achieves $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.94$ at 10\% training progress for distinguishing $\alpha = 1.0$ from $\alpha = 0$, reaching $0.984$ over the full run (Figure~\ref{fig:roc_curves}; Table~\ref{tab:within_gen_roc}).

50	
51	
52	\paragraph{Spectral and token entropy.}

56	\paragraph{Train loss: effective but interpretively ambiguous.}

61	Train loss is therefore unreliable as an early collapse alarm (AUROC below chance for the first ${\sim}20\%$ of training), but effective at completion.
62	Practitioners should cross-validate with spectral indicators such as stable rank, which achieves $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.94$ from 10\% progress onward.
63	
64	\paragraph{Evaluation perplexity: no within-generation signal.}

66	This failure has a structural explanation: within a single generation, the model trains on a fixed corpus $\mathcal{D}_g$ and has not yet produced the synthetic data that will contaminate $\mathcal{D}_{g+1}$ (Eq.~\ref{eq:mixing}).

77	\label{sec:taxonomy}

A more actionable capability is detecting collapse \emph{within} a single training run, enabling early stopping before degradation accumulates.

\paragraph{Stable rank as early alarm.}
Stable rank achieves $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.94$ at 10\% training progress for distinguishing $\alpha = 1.0$ from $\alpha = 0$, reaching $0.984$ over the full run (Figure~\ref{fig:roc_curves}; Table~\ref{tab:within_gen_roc}).
At step~50 (3\% of training), $\Delta_\mathrm{SR} = 34.4\%$---far exceeding the 5\% detection threshold defined in Section~\ref{sec:evaluation}.
Stable rank's within-generation sensitivity reflects the structural nature of spectral signals: contamination alters the covariance eigenspectrum before output-level metrics respond, because energy dispersal across representation dimensions (Eq.~\ref{eq:stable_rank}) is detectable even when the model's token-level predictions have not yet degraded.


\paragraph{Spectral and token entropy.}
Token entropy deviates 24.5\% at step~50 but achieves only $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.478$ (pooled)---near random chance, indicating that despite its large initial deviation, token entropy provides no reliable within-generation discrimination.
Spectral entropy achieves pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.773$, providing moderate within-generation discrimination but still substantially below stable rank's pooled $0.984$.

Evaluation perplexity accumulates degradation \emph{across} generations through the iterative contamination loop, not within a single run.
Consequently, it does not diverge from baseline within one generation, even when collapse is underway.

Spectral signals, by contrast, detect structural change---the dispersal of representational energy across dimensions---independent of whether the model's held-out predictions have degraded.
This yields a three-level hierarchy of within-generation detection capability (all pooled AUROC): stable rank ($0.984$) detects changes in weight-space structure, train loss ($0.923$) detects changes in training data distribution, and held-out evaluation perplexity ($0.533$) measures generalization quality---which does not diverge within a single generation.

\label{sec:taxonomy}

The cross-method comparison (C1 vs C4; Table~\ref{tab:configs}) reveals that the same signal can be informative under one training method and misleading under another.

\paragraph{Gradient norm: method-dependent.}
Under QLoRA, gradient norm changes non-monotonically with contamination: $+5.9\%$ at $\alpha = 0.5$ relative to baseline, then $-30.8\%$ at $\alpha = 1.0$.
Under full fine-tuning, gradient norm decreases monotonically ($-58.3\%$ at $\alpha = 1.0$), consistent with the model converging more easily to lower-entropy synthetic data.
The QLoRA non-monotonicity likely arises from the interaction between contaminated gradients and the rank-$r$ adapter subspace~\citep{hu2022lora}: at moderate contamination, gradients from mixed real/synthetic data create conflicting update directions within the low-rank projection, inflating the norm; at full contamination, the uniform synthetic signal reduces this conflict~\citep{dettmers2023qlora}.
This method-dependence means gradient norm cannot be used as a collapse indicator without knowing the training configuration (Figure~\ref{fig:signal_heatmap}).

\paragraph{Downstream and diversity metrics: insensitive at 0.5B.}
HellaSwag accuracy is insensitive under QLoRA (relative change $-1.15\%$; $N=1$ seed at 0.5B, no effect size computable).
Under full fine-tuning, the $\alpha = 0$ baseline is unavailable, preventing direct effect size computation; the available data show accuracy of $0.397$ ($\alpha = 0.5$) and $0.372$ ($\alpha = 1.0$), a $-6.3\%$ relative change between these two conditions.

Distinct-1 is non-monotonic under QLoRA: $+17.7\%$ at $\alpha = 0.5$ but $-12.5\%$ at $\alpha = 1.0$, reversing direction between moderate and full contamination.
Self-BLEU is insensitive to collapse even when evaluation perplexity increases $17\times$.
This disconnect arises because nucleus sampling ($p = 0.95$) draws from the distribution tail, producing superficially diverse surface forms even as the model's probability mass concentrates on fewer modes.
Token entropy captures this concentration (Section~\ref{sec:correlation}), but $n$-gram diversity metrics do not.
Monitoring pipelines that rely solely on output diversity metrics risk missing collapse entirely.

\paragraph{Full fine-tuning collapse dynamics.}
Full fine-tuning produces sharper onset but lower terminal severity than QLoRA (Figure~\ref{fig:method_comparison}).
The generation~0 to generation~1 evaluation perplexity ratio is $15.3\times$ under full FT versus $8.7\times$ under QLoRA.
Post-onset, the trajectory is non-monotonic: evaluation perplexity \emph{decreases} from $294.0$ at generation~1 to $288.5$ at generation~2 before rising through generations~3--4 to a terminal value of $326.19$.
This generation~2 dip echoes the partial recovery observed at moderate contamination (Section~\ref{sec:taxonomy}), suggesting that full parameter access allows transient re-adaptation even under full synthetic pressure.
The overall generation~1 to generation~4 ratio remains $1.11\times$, compared to continued monotonic growth under QLoRA, and terminal severity is lower: $\mathrm{PPL}_\text{eval} = 326.19$ versus QLoRA's $839.2$ ($0.39\times$).
This pattern---fast onset, partial dip, then resumed rise at lower terminal severity---is consistent with full parameter access enabling rapid adaptation to synthetic data characteristics.

We observe that terminal stable rank values are similar across methods: $\mathrm{SR} = 153.87$ (full FT) versus $155.64$ (QLoRA) at generation~4, $\alpha = 1.0$.
This comparison rests on $N = 1$ seed per method and cannot be distinguished from coincidence; we note it as an observation, not a finding.

\paragraph{Partial recovery at moderate contamination.}
At $\alpha = 0.5$, signals show partial recovery across generations relative to the $\alpha = 1.0$ trajectory.
Output signals (evaluation perplexity, token entropy) recover approximately 52\% of the clean-to-collapsed gap, while weight-space signals (stable rank, spectral entropy) recover approximately 33\%.
This pattern is consistent with data accumulation effects~\citep{Gerstgrasser2024}: the retained real data fraction attenuates collapse pressure.
Recovery ratios are computed within each signal family; cross-family prevalence comparisons are not meaningful because the signals have different scales and sensitivity profiles.

\paragraph{Recommended operating ranges.}
Based on the evidence above, we propose signal-to-task assignments (Table~\ref{tab:signal_taxonomy}):
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
    \item \textbf{Within-generation alarm:} stable rank ($\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.94$ at 10\% progress, $0.984$ pooled).
    \item \textbf{Cross-generation severity discrimination:} spectral entropy ($d = 33.48$, $\mathrm{CV} = 0.0015$).
    \item \textbf{Cross-generation tracking:} evaluation perplexity (large absolute effect, interpretable scale).
    \item \textbf{Method-dependent:} gradient norm (monotonic under full FT only).
    \item \textbf{Non-monotonic:} distinct-1 ($+17.7\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.5$, $-12.5\%$ at $\alpha{=}1.0$ under QLoRA).
    \item \textbf{Insensitive at 0.5B scale:} HellaSwag accuracy (relative change ${<}3\%$, $N{=}1$).
\end{itemize}

Effect sizes in Section~\ref{sec:correlation} are from C2 (1.5B, $N=3$ interim seeds); within-generation AUROC values are from C1 (0.5B, $N=1$ seed); method-dependent operating ranges are from C1 vs C4 (0.5B, $N=1$ seed each).
Validation across larger models, additional domains, and larger seed counts is required before these operating ranges can be considered robust.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We presented a systematic empirical study of training-time signals as model collapse severity monitors.
Across five experimental configurations spanning two model scales (0.5B--3B), two text domains (WikiText-2, PubMed), two fine-tuning methods (QLoRA, full fine-tuning), and six contamination fractions, we established three findings.

First, spectral and output signals reliably track collapse severity across configurations.
Spectral entropy achieves the largest and most reproducible effect size ($d = 33.48$, $\mathrm{CV} = 0.0015$ across seeds), followed by evaluation perplexity ($d = 20.82$) and stable rank ($d = 9.43$, $\mathrm{CV} = 0.022$).
Six of seven monitored signals maintain consistent direction of change regardless of training method.

Second, stable rank provides within-generation early warning, achieving $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.94$ at 10\% training progress ($0.984$ pooled) and 34.4\% deviation from baseline at 3\% of training.
Train loss provides the second-strongest within-generation signal (pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.923$), though its decrease reflects successful fitting of corrupted data rather than improved model quality.
Held-out evaluation perplexity (pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.533$) and token entropy (pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.478$) fail at within-generation detection---the most commonly relied-upon quality metric is no better than chance at the most actionable task.

Third, signal informativeness depends on the fine-tuning method and model scale, motivating a three-tier monitoring strategy: stable rank for within-generation alarms, evaluation perplexity for cross-generation tracking, and spectral entropy for severity discrimination.

\paragraph{Future directions.}
Validating these findings at scales of practical interest ($\geq$7B) and across diverse domains would establish generalizability.
Translating early warning signals into automated intervention triggers---adaptive learning rate reduction, selective data filtering, or training rollback when spectral deviation exceeds calibrated thresholds---would close the loop from detection to mitigation.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

As LLM-generated text pervades web-scraped training corpora, practitioners increasingly fine-tune models on data shaped by prior model generations.
This recursive dynamic creates self-consuming loops that cause \emph{model collapse}---progressive loss of distribution tails, contraction of output diversity, and degradation of acquired knowledge~\citep{Shumailov2024,Alemohammad2024}.
The problem compounds: even trace synthetic contamination induces collapse at sufficient depth~\citep{Dohmatob2025}, with errors accumulating across iterations at accelerating rates~\citep{Dohmatob2024_tails,Fu2024_icml}.
Yet the metric practitioners most commonly rely on for quality assessment---held-out evaluation perplexity---fails to detect this degradation within a run, achieving pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.533$ for within-generation collapse detection (indistinguishable from random chance).
Train loss does change under collapse (pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.923$), but its decrease is interpretively ambiguous: the model fits lower-entropy synthetic data more easily, which looks like healthy convergence.
A practitioner watching only perplexity or interpreting train loss at face value would have no reliable warning that collapse is underway.

Existing work addresses model collapse from two directions.
On the theoretical side, \citet{Shumailov2024} established the phenomenon, \citet{Dohmatob2025} proved that any nonzero synthetic fraction eventually induces strong collapse, and \citet{Dohmatob2024_tails} showed that collapse alters neural scaling laws.
On the mitigation side, data accumulation~\citep{Gerstgrasser2024}, loss modification~\citep{Zibakhsh2025}, and verification-based filtering~\citep{Feng2025} each reduce collapse pressure under specific conditions.
Missing from this landscape is a systematic analysis of which \emph{training-time signals} best track collapse severity, when they provide early warning, and where they saturate or actively mislead.
\citet{Schaeffer2025} highlight that even the definition of collapse varies across studies, further motivating signal-level analysis grounded in controlled experiments.
The two closest concurrent works---SIGMA~\citep{Gu2026}, which monitors output embedding spectra, and the topological index of \citet{Kalinowski2026}---each address part of this gap but carry limitations: SIGMA requires a clean reference distribution and operates post-hoc; topological monitoring incurs higher computational cost.
Neither provides a cross-family comparison of signal operating ranges or quantitative within-generation early warning thresholds.

We conduct a systematic empirical study of training-time signals as collapse severity monitors.
We evaluate four signal families---spectral (stable rank, spectral entropy), output (train loss, evaluation perplexity, token entropy), gradient (L2 norm), and downstream (HellaSwag accuracy)---across five experimental configurations spanning model scales (0.5B to 3B), fine-tuning methods (QLoRA and full fine-tuning), contamination fractions ($\alpha \in \{0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0\}$), and text domains (WikiText-2, PubMed).
Our central finding is that different signal families have complementary operating ranges, and the same signal's utility can flip from informative to misleading depending on the training method.

Our contributions:

\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Signal--severity correlation.}
    Spectral and output signals track collapse across contamination levels.
    Spectral entropy achieves the largest effect size (Cohen's $d = 33.48$, coefficient of variation $\mathrm{CV} = 0.0015$ across seeds), followed by evaluation perplexity ($d = 20.82$) and stable rank ($d = 9.43$, $\mathrm{CV} = 0.022$).
    Validated across QLoRA and full fine-tuning, six of seven monitored signals maintain consistent direction of change regardless of training method.
    The exception---gradient norm, which is non-monotonic under QLoRA but monotonic under full fine-tuning---demonstrates that method-dependence is a first-order concern for monitoring pipeline design.

    \item \textbf{Within-generation early warning and negative results.}
    Stable rank achieves $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.94$ at 10\% training progress ($0.984$ pooled) for binary collapse detection, with 34.4\% deviation from baseline at 3\% of training.
    Train loss provides the second-strongest within-generation signal (pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.923$), though its decrease reflects successful fitting of corrupted data rather than improved model quality.
    Held-out evaluation perplexity achieves pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.533$ for within-generation detection---the most commonly relied-upon quality metric fails at the most actionable task---and token entropy achieves pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.478$, providing no reliable discrimination despite a large initial deviation.
    Evaluation perplexity's failure has a structural explanation: it accumulates degradation through the iterative contamination loop, not within a single generation's training.

    \item \textbf{Signal taxonomy with method-dependent operating ranges.}
    Signal informativeness depends on the fine-tuning method and model scale.
    Gradient norm is non-monotonic under QLoRA but monotonic under full fine-tuning.
    HellaSwag accuracy is insensitive at 0.5B scale (relative change ${<}3\%$, $N{=}1$).
    Distinct-1 is non-monotonic, reversing direction between moderate and full contamination.
    Full fine-tuning produces sharper collapse onset ($15.3\times$ evaluation perplexity ratio at generation~1) than QLoRA ($8.7\times$) but lower terminal severity.
    These findings motivate a three-tier recommendation: stable rank for within-generation alarms, evaluation perplexity for cross-generation tracking, and spectral entropy for severity discrimination.
\end{enumerate}

Section~\ref{sec:related_work} surveys collapse theory, spectral analysis of neural networks, and concurrent monitoring approaches.
Section~\ref{sec:method} details our iterative contamination protocol, signal definitions, and evaluation framework.
Section~\ref{sec:results} presents signal--severity correlations, within-generation early warning analysis, and the method-dependent signal taxonomy.
Section~\ref{sec:discussion} discusses practical monitoring recommendations and limitations.
Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We presented a systematic empirical study of training-time signals as model collapse severity monitors.
Across three experimental configurations spanning two model scales (0.5B, 1.5B), two fine-tuning methods (QLoRA, full fine-tuning), and six contamination fractions on WikiText-2, we established three findings.

First, spectral and output signals reliably track collapse severity across configurations.
Spectral entropy achieves the largest and most reproducible effect size ($d = 33.48$, $\mathrm{CV} = 0.0015$ across seeds), followed by evaluation perplexity ($d = 20.82$) and stable rank ($d = 9.43$, $\mathrm{CV} = 0.022$).
Six of seven monitored signals maintain consistent direction of change regardless of training method.

Second, stable rank provides within-generation early warning, achieving $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.94$ at 10\% training progress ($0.984$ pooled) and 34.4\% deviation from baseline at 3\% of training.
Train loss provides the second-strongest within-generation signal (pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.923$), though its decrease reflects successful fitting of corrupted data rather than improved model quality.
Held-out evaluation perplexity (pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.533$) and token entropy (pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.478$) fail at within-generation detection---the most commonly relied-upon quality metric is no better than chance at the most actionable task.

Third, signal informativeness depends on the fine-tuning method and model scale, motivating a three-tier monitoring strategy: stable rank for within-generation alarms, evaluation perplexity for cross-generation tracking, and spectral entropy for severity discrimination.

\paragraph{Future directions.}
Validating these findings at scales of practical interest ($\geq$7B) and across diverse domains would establish generalizability.
Translating early warning signals into automated intervention triggers---adaptive learning rate reduction, selective data filtering, or training rollback when spectral deviation exceeds calibrated thresholds---would close the loop from detection to mitigation.

% Limitations section — collapse_severity_monitor

Our study has several limitations that bound the scope of our conclusions.

\paragraph{Scale.}
Our primary experiments use Qwen2.5-0.5B and 1.5B models, with only a single-seed spot-check at 3B.
Whether signal--severity relationships and operating ranges transfer to models at scales of practical deployment ($\geq$7B) remains unvalidated.
Stable rank baselines are known to be scale-dependent~\citep{Jha2025}, and threshold calibration may require per-scale adjustment.

\paragraph{Seed count and statistical power.}
Cross-generation effect sizes are computed from $N = 3$ seeds (C2 configuration, interim 3 of 5 planned seeds); within-generation AUROC results use $N = 1$ seed at 0.5B (C1).
The full fine-tuning comparison (C4) uses $N = 1$ seed.
These sample sizes are insufficient for rank-based tests (minimum $p = 0.25$ for Wilcoxon with $N = 3$), and we rely on bootstrap confidence intervals.
Stable rank's coefficient of variation ($\mathrm{CV} = 0.022$) is an order of magnitude larger than spectral entropy's ($0.0015$), and its effect size dropped from $d = 61.7$ to $d = 9.43$ when a third seed was added---underscoring that our ranking of signals by sensitivity may shift with more seeds.

\paragraph{Domain coverage.}
We evaluate on WikiText-2 and PubMed abstracts.
Whether our signal taxonomy generalizes to code, dialogue, multilingual text, or instruction-following data is unknown.

\paragraph{Collapse source.}
Our iterative retraining protocol simulates a specific collapse mechanism---self-consuming loops with controlled contamination fractions.
Real-world collapse may involve mixed provenance (multiple model generations), distribution shift between generations, or partial synthetic contamination at unknown fractions.
Signal behavior under these conditions may differ from our controlled setting.

\paragraph{Fine-tuning methods.}
We compare QLoRA and full fine-tuning.
Other parameter-efficient methods (LoRA without quantization, adapters, prefix tuning) may interact differently with spectral signals due to different parameterization constraints.

\paragraph{Causal claims.}
We establish correlations between signals and collapse severity, not causal mechanisms.
The spectral entropy increase under collapse reflects a change in representation structure, but we do not prove that this change causes (rather than accompanies) output degradation.

1	\section{Related Work}
2	\label{sec:related_work}
3	
4	\paragraph{Model collapse in iterative training.}
5	Model collapse---progressive degradation when models train on their own outputs---has been established across generative families~\citep{Shumailov2024,Alemohammad2024}.
6	Theoretical analyses show that even trace synthetic contamination induces collapse~\citep{Dohmatob2025}, with errors compounding across iterations~\citep{Dohmatob2024_tails,Fu2024_icml}, altered scaling laws~\citep{Seddik2024}, and entropy-driven memorization transitions~\citep{Shi2025_neurips}.
7	\citet{Schaeffer2025} catalogued eight distinct collapse definitions, motivating precise operationalization.
8	Mitigation strategies include data accumulation~\citep{Gerstgrasser2024,Kazdan2024}, loss modification~\citep{Zibakhsh2025}, verification-based filtering~\citep{Feng2025,Yi2025}, and correction functions~\citep{Gillman2024,Bakshi2026}.
9	These works establish \emph{that} collapse occurs and \emph{how} to mitigate it, but rely on post-hoc evaluation; none provides real-time training-time monitoring.
10	
11	\paragraph{Spectral and training-dynamic diagnostics.}
12	Spectral properties of weight matrices predict model quality without test data~\citep{Martin2021}, with stable rank linked to generalization~\citep{Sanyal2020} and shown to be scale-dependent~\citep{Jha2025}.
13	Recent work has characterized spectral dynamics across training~\citep{Liu2026_lifecycle,Staats2024,Pennington2017}, used spectral signals for compression and pruning~\citep{Xu2026,AlphaPruning2024,Yunis2024}, and applied gradient-based diagnostics~\citep{Li2025_gradient,Elgaar2026}, diffusion spectral entropy~\citep{Chen2024_dse}, spectral alignment~\citep{Qiu2025}, and loss landscape curvature~\citep{Kalra2026} to training health monitoring.
14	
15	\paragraph{Closest concurrent work.}
16	SIGMA~\citep{Gu2026} analyzes the output embedding Gram matrix spectrum to quantify collapse but operates post-hoc, requires a clean reference distribution, and has not been validated in iterative settings.
17	\citet{Kalinowski2026} proposes an online topological monitor via persistent homology but uses a different signal family and incurs higher computational cost (Table~\ref{tab:competitor_comparison} in Appendix~\ref{app:competitor_comparison}).
18	Neither provides a cross-family comparison, documents where signals saturate or mislead, or establishes within-generation early warning thresholds.
19	
20	\paragraph{Data quality and contamination detection.}
21	Watermarking~\citep{Kirchenbauer2023,Dathathri2024,Sander2024} and statistical detection~\citep{Mitchell2023,Shi2024_mink} identify synthetic data presence, while dataset-level approaches address quality filtering~\citep{Penedo2024,Zhang2026} and diversity quantification~\citep{Gambetta2024,Wang2025_scaling}.
22	These methods answer whether synthetic data is \emph{present}; our work addresses how severely it has \emph{degraded} the model, operating in real time during training rather than post-hoc.
23	Across the literature, no prior work simultaneously achieves online monitoring, spectral/entropic training-dynamic signals, per-layer granularity, and validation in the iterative synthetic data setting.

% Results section — collapse_severity_monitor
% Data sources: plan006 (3-seed Cohen's d), within_gen_analysis, plan003-fullft-05B, heatmap_data.json

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

We organize results around three claims.
Section~\ref{sec:correlation} establishes that spectral and output signals track collapse severity across configurations.
Section~\ref{sec:early_warning_results} shows that certain signals detect collapse within a single training run before evaluation perplexity diverges.
Section~\ref{sec:taxonomy} reveals that signal informativeness depends on the fine-tuning method, motivating a taxonomy of method-dependent operating ranges.

\subsection{Signal--Severity Correlation}
\label{sec:correlation}

We quantify signal sensitivity using Cohen's $d$ between the clean baseline ($\alpha = 0$) and full contamination ($\alpha = 1.0$) at generation~4, computed across three seeds from the C2 configuration (Qwen2.5-1.5B, WikiText-2; interim 3 of 5 planned seeds; Table~\ref{tab:configs}).
Effect sizes, rather than rank correlations, serve as the primary evidence because they convey the magnitude of signal separation, not just its ordering.

\paragraph{Effect sizes.}
Spectral entropy achieves the largest and most reproducible effect size ($d = 33.48$, coefficient of variation across seeds $\mathrm{CV} = 0.0015$), followed by evaluation perplexity ($d = 20.82$), distinct-1 ($d = 14.60$, 1.5B, effective $N=2$ seeds; this large endpoint separation coexists with non-monotonic intermediate behavior at 0.5B, Section~\ref{sec:taxonomy}), and stable rank ($d = 9.43$, $\mathrm{CV} = 0.022$).
Distinct-2 ($d = 7.59$) and distinct-3 ($d = -7.08$; negative because collapse increases trigram repetition) provide moderate separation.
Token entropy, self-BLEU, gradient norm, and HellaSwag accuracy yield small effect sizes ($d < 5$), placing them in a second tier for cross-generation severity discrimination (Figure~\ref{fig:severity_curves}).

Stable rank warrants a cautionary note on seed sensitivity.
With two seeds, $d = 61.7$; adding a third seed reduced this to $d = 9.43$---a rank change from 1st to 4th among monitored signals.
Its $\mathrm{CV}$ of 0.022 is an order of magnitude larger than spectral entropy's 0.0015.
We treat stable rank as informative but seed-sensitive at this sample size; $N = 3$ seeds are insufficient for a Wilcoxon test (minimum $p = 0.25$), and we rely on bootstrap confidence intervals for inference.


\paragraph{Cross-method consistency.}
Six of seven monitored signals maintain consistent direction of change under both QLoRA and full fine-tuning (Figure~\ref{fig:signal_heatmap}): spectral entropy, stable rank, evaluation perplexity, token entropy, distinct-1, and self-BLEU all move in the same direction as contamination increases, regardless of training method.
The exception is gradient norm, which exhibits non-monotonic behavior under QLoRA but monotonic decrease under full fine-tuning (Section~\ref{sec:taxonomy}).

\paragraph{Supporting rank correlations.}
Spearman correlations provide directional confirmation: spectral entropy maintains high $|\rho|$ across generations.
However, $|\rho| = 1.0$ for stable rank across contamination fractions is trivially achieved with few contamination levels and should not be interpreted as strong evidence of monotonicity.
We therefore use Cohen's $d$ as the primary sensitivity measure throughout.


\subsection{Within-Generation Early Warning}
\label{sec:early_warning_results}

Cross-generation tracking (Section~\ref{sec:correlation}) requires completing multiple generations to assess severity.
A more actionable capability is detecting collapse \emph{within} a single training run, enabling early stopping before degradation accumulates.
We evaluate this using the relative deviation $\Delta_s$ (Eq.~\ref{eq:deviation}) and AUROC for binary collapse detection at each checkpoint.

\paragraph{Stable rank as early alarm.}
Stable rank achieves $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.94$ at 10\% training progress for distinguishing $\alpha = 1.0$ from $\alpha = 0$, reaching $0.984$ over the full run (Figure~\ref{fig:roc_curves}; Table~\ref{tab:within_gen_roc}).
At step~50 (3\% of training), $\Delta_\mathrm{SR} = 34.4\%$---far exceeding the 5\% detection threshold defined in Section~\ref{sec:evaluation}.
Stable rank's within-generation sensitivity reflects the structural nature of spectral signals: contamination alters the covariance eigenspectrum before output-level metrics respond, because energy dispersal across representation dimensions (Eq.~\ref{eq:stable_rank}) is detectable even when the model's token-level predictions have not yet degraded.


\paragraph{Spectral and token entropy.}
Token entropy deviates 24.5\% at step~50 but achieves only $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.478$ (pooled)---near random chance, indicating that despite its large initial deviation, token entropy provides no reliable within-generation discrimination.
Spectral entropy achieves pooled $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.773$, providing moderate within-generation discrimination but still substantially below stable rank's pooled $0.984$.

\paragraph{Train loss: effective but interpretively ambiguous.}
Train loss achieves $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.923$ at training completion, the second-strongest within-generation signal after stable rank.
However, its AUROC trajectory reveals early-training direction reversal (Figure~\ref{fig:roc_curves}b): $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.24$ at 10\% progress, rising to $0.48$ at 20\%, $0.85$ at 50\%, and $0.923$ at completion.
The low early AUROC (${<}\,0.5$) indicates that the collapsing run's training loss is initially \emph{lower} than the clean baseline---the model fits the lower-entropy synthetic distribution more easily, a direct manifestation of the collapse mechanism.
As training progresses, cumulative degradation raises loss in the collapsed run, gradually restoring discriminability.
Train loss is therefore unreliable as an early collapse alarm (AUROC below chance for the first ${\sim}20\%$ of training), but effective at completion.
Practitioners should cross-validate with spectral indicators such as stable rank, which achieves $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.94$ from 10\% progress onward.

\paragraph{Evaluation perplexity: no within-generation signal.}
Held-out evaluation perplexity achieves only $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.533$ across the full run---indistinguishable from random.
This failure has a structural explanation: within a single generation, the model trains on a fixed corpus $\mathcal{D}_g$ and has not yet produced the synthetic data that will contaminate $\mathcal{D}_{g+1}$ (Eq.~\ref{eq:mixing}).
Evaluation perplexity accumulates degradation \emph{across} generations through the iterative contamination loop, not within a single run.
Consequently, it does not diverge from baseline within one generation, even when collapse is underway.

Spectral signals, by contrast, detect structural change---the dispersal of representational energy across dimensions---independent of whether the model's held-out predictions have degraded.
This yields a three-level hierarchy of within-generation detection capability (all pooled AUROC): stable rank ($0.984$) detects changes in representation-space structure, train loss ($0.923$) detects changes in training data distribution, and held-out evaluation perplexity ($0.533$) measures generalization quality---which does not diverge within a single generation.
The weakest link in within-generation monitoring is precisely the metric practitioners most commonly check at evaluation checkpoints.



\subsection{Signal Taxonomy: Method-Dependent Operating Ranges}
\label{sec:taxonomy}

The cross-method comparison (C1 vs C4; Table~\ref{tab:configs}) reveals that the same signal can be informative under one training method and misleading under another.

\paragraph{Gradient norm: method-dependent.}
Under QLoRA, gradient norm changes non-monotonically with contamination: $+5.9\%$ at $\alpha = 0.5$ relative to baseline, then $-30.8\%$ at $\alpha = 1.0$.
Under full fine-tuning, gradient norm decreases monotonically ($-58.3\%$ at $\alpha = 1.0$), consistent with the model converging more easily to lower-entropy synthetic data.
The QLoRA non-monotonicity likely arises from the interaction between contaminated gradients and the rank-$r$ adapter subspace~\citep{hu2022lora}: at moderate contamination, gradients from mixed real/synthetic data create conflicting update directions within the low-rank projection, inflating the norm; at full contamination, the uniform synthetic signal reduces this conflict~\citep{dettmers2023qlora}.
This method-dependence means gradient norm cannot be used as a collapse indicator without knowing the training configuration (Figure~\ref{fig:signal_heatmap}).

\paragraph{Downstream and diversity metrics: insensitive at 0.5B.}
HellaSwag accuracy is insensitive under QLoRA (relative change $-1.15\%$; $N=1$ seed at 0.5B, no effect size computable).
Under full fine-tuning, the $\alpha = 0$ baseline is unavailable, preventing direct effect size computation; the available data show accuracy of $0.397$ ($\alpha = 0.5$) and $0.372$ ($\alpha = 1.0$), a $-6.3\%$ relative change between these two conditions.

Distinct-1 is non-monotonic under QLoRA: $+17.7\%$ at $\alpha = 0.5$ but $-12.5\%$ at $\alpha = 1.0$, reversing direction between moderate and full contamination.
Self-BLEU is insensitive to collapse even when evaluation perplexity increases $17\times$.
This disconnect arises because nucleus sampling ($p = 0.95$) draws from the distribution tail, producing superficially diverse surface forms even as the model's probability mass concentrates on fewer modes.
Token entropy captures this concentration (Section~\ref{sec:correlation}), but $n$-gram diversity metrics do not.
Monitoring pipelines that rely solely on output diversity metrics risk missing collapse entirely.

\paragraph{Full fine-tuning collapse dynamics.}
Full fine-tuning produces sharper onset but lower terminal severity than QLoRA (Figure~\ref{fig:method_comparison}).
The generation~0 to generation~1 evaluation perplexity ratio is $15.3\times$ under full FT versus $8.7\times$ under QLoRA.
Post-onset, the trajectory is non-monotonic: evaluation perplexity \emph{decreases} from $294.0$ at generation~1 to $288.5$ at generation~2 before rising through generations~3--4 to a terminal value of $326.19$.
This generation~2 dip echoes the partial recovery observed at moderate contamination (Section~\ref{sec:taxonomy}), suggesting that full parameter access allows transient re-adaptation even under full synthetic pressure.
The overall generation~1 to generation~4 ratio remains $1.11\times$, compared to continued monotonic growth under QLoRA, and terminal severity is lower: $\mathrm{PPL}_\text{eval} = 326.19$ versus QLoRA's $839.2$ ($0.39\times$).
This pattern---fast onset, partial dip, then resumed rise at lower terminal severity---is consistent with full parameter access enabling rapid adaptation to synthetic data characteristics.

We observe that terminal stable rank values are similar across methods: $\mathrm{SR} = 153.87$ (full FT) versus $155.64$ (QLoRA) at generation~4, $\alpha = 1.0$.
This comparison rests on $N = 1$ seed per method and cannot be distinguished from coincidence; we note it as an observation, not a finding.

\paragraph{Partial recovery at moderate contamination.}
At $\alpha = 0.5$, signals show partial recovery across generations relative to the $\alpha = 1.0$ trajectory.

% Limitations section — collapse_severity_monitor

Our study has several limitations that bound the scope of our conclusions.

\paragraph{Scale.}
All reported results use Qwen2.5-0.5B and 1.5B models.
Scale validation at 3B and cross-domain validation on PubMed are ongoing but not yet complete.
Whether signal--severity relationships and operating ranges transfer to models at scales of practical deployment ($\geq$7B) remains unvalidated.
Stable rank baselines are known to be scale-dependent~\citep{Jha2025}, and threshold calibration may require per-scale adjustment.

\paragraph{Seed count and statistical power.}

\paragraph{Domain coverage.}
All reported results use WikiText-2; cross-domain validation on PubMed is ongoing.
Whether our signal taxonomy generalizes to biomedical text, code, dialogue, multilingual text, or instruction-following data is unknown.

\paragraph{Collapse source.}
Our iterative retraining protocol simulates a specific collapse mechanism---self-consuming loops with controlled contamination fractions.
Real-world collapse may involve mixed provenance (multiple model generations), distribution shift between generations, or partial synthetic contamination at unknown fractions.
Signal behavior under these conditions may differ from our controlled setting.

\paragraph{Fine-tuning methods.}
We compare QLoRA and full fine-tuning.
Other parameter-efficient methods (LoRA without quantization, adapters, prefix tuning) may interact differently with spectral signals due to different parameterization constraints.

\paragraph{Causal claims.}
We establish correlations between signals and collapse severity, not causal mechanisms.
The spectral entropy increase under collapse reflects a change in representation structure, but we do not prove that this change causes (rather than accompanies) output degradation.

4	\paragraph{Model collapse in iterative training.}
5	Model collapse---progressive degradation when models train on their own outputs---has been established across generative families~\citep{Shumailov2024,Alemohammad2024}.
6	Theoretical analyses show that even trace synthetic contamination induces collapse~\citep{Dohmatob2025}, with errors compounding across iterations~\citep{Dohmatob2024_tails,Fu2024_icml}, altered scaling laws~\citep{Seddik2024}, and entropy-driven memorization transitions~\citep{Shi2025_neurips}.
7	\citet{Schaeffer2025} catalogued eight distinct collapse definitions, motivating precise operationalization.
8	Mitigation strategies include data accumulation~\citep{Gerstgrasser2024,Kazdan2024}, loss modification~\citep{Zibakhsh2025}, verification-based filtering~\citep{Feng2025,Yi2025}, and correction functions~\citep{Gillman2024,Bakshi2026}.
9	These works establish \emph{that} collapse occurs and \emph{how} to mitigate it, but rely on post-hoc evaluation; none provides real-time training-time monitoring.
10	
11	\paragraph{Spectral and training-dynamic diagnostics.}
12	Spectral properties of weight matrices predict model quality without test data~\citep{Martin2021}, with stable rank linked to generalization~\citep{Sanyal2020} and shown to be scale-dependent~\citep{Jha2025}.

14	
15	\paragraph{Closest concurrent work.}

Distinct-1 is non-monotonic under QLoRA: $+17.7\%$ at $\alpha = 0.5$ but $-12.5\%$ at $\alpha = 1.0$, reversing direction between moderate and full contamination.
Self-BLEU is insensitive to collapse even when evaluation perplexity increases $17\times$.
This disconnect arises because nucleus sampling ($p = 0.95$) draws from the distribution tail, producing superficially diverse surface forms even as the model's probability mass concentrates on fewer modes.
Token entropy captures this concentration (Section~\ref{sec:correlation}), but $n$-gram diversity metrics do not.
Monitoring pipelines that rely solely on output diversity metrics risk missing collapse entirely.

\paragraph{Full fine-tuning collapse dynamics.}
Full fine-tuning produces sharper onset but lower terminal severity than QLoRA (Figure~\ref{fig:method_comparison}).
The generation~0 to generation~1 evaluation perplexity ratio is $15.3\times$ under full FT versus $8.7\times$ under QLoRA.
Post-onset, the trajectory is non-monotonic: evaluation perplexity \emph{decreases} from $294.0$ at generation~1 to $288.5$ at generation~2 before rising through generations~3--4 to a terminal value of $326.19$.
This generation~2 dip echoes the partial recovery observed at moderate contamination (Section~\ref{sec:taxonomy}), suggesting that full parameter access allows transient re-adaptation even under full synthetic pressure.
The overall generation~1 to generation~4 ratio remains $1.11\times$, compared to continued monotonic growth under QLoRA, and terminal severity is lower: $\mathrm{PPL}_\text{eval} = 326.19$ versus QLoRA's $839.2$ ($0.39\times$).
This pattern---fast onset, partial dip, then resumed rise at lower terminal severity---is consistent with full parameter access enabling rapid adaptation to synthetic data characteristics.

We observe that terminal stable rank values are similar across methods: $\mathrm{SR} = 153.87$ (full FT) versus $155.64$ (QLoRA) at generation~4, $\alpha = 1.0$.
This comparison rests on $N = 1$ seed per method and cannot be distinguished from coincidence; we note it as an observation, not a finding.

\paragraph{Partial recovery at moderate contamination.}
At $\alpha = 0.5$, signals show partial recovery across generations relative to the $\alpha = 1.0$ trajectory.
Output signals (evaluation perplexity, token entropy) recover approximately 52\% of the clean-to-collapsed gap, while representation-space signals (stable rank, spectral entropy) recover approximately 33\%.
This pattern is consistent with data accumulation effects~\citep{Gerstgrasser2024}: the retained real data fraction attenuates collapse pressure.
Recovery ratios are computed within each signal family; cross-family prevalence comparisons are not meaningful because the signals have different scales and sensitivity profiles.

\paragraph{Recommended operating ranges.}
Based on the evidence above, we propose signal-to-task assignments (Table~\ref{tab:signal_taxonomy}):
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
    \item \textbf{Within-generation alarm:} stable rank ($\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.94$ at 10\% progress, $0.984$ pooled).
    \item \textbf{Cross-generation severity discrimination:} spectral entropy ($d = 33.48$, $\mathrm{CV} = 0.0015$).
    \item \textbf{Cross-generation tracking:} evaluation perplexity (large absolute effect, interpretable scale).
    \item \textbf{Method-dependent:} gradient norm (monotonic under full FT only).
    \item \textbf{Non-monotonic:} distinct-1 ($+17.7\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.5$, $-12.5\%$ at $\alpha{=}1.0$ under QLoRA).
    \item \textbf{Insensitive at 0.5B scale:} HellaSwag accuracy (relative change ${<}3\%$, $N{=}1$).
\end{itemize}

\noindent
Effect sizes in Section~\ref{sec:correlation} are from C2 (1.5B, $N=3$ interim seeds); within-generation AUROC values are from C1 (0.5B, $N=1$ seed); method-dependent operating ranges are from C1 vs C4 (0.5B, $N=1$ seed each).
Validation across larger models, additional domains, and larger seed counts is required before these operating ranges can be considered robust.
